newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Text or RBNZ news release on Alliance meeting.
newsitem.headline: Text or RBNZ news release on Alliance meeting.

text.p: The Alliance caucus may have misunderstood the point I was making when I gave them a confidential background briefing yesterday, Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said today.

This follows Alliance leader Jim Anderton being reported as having said that Dr Brash yesterday told the Alliance caucus that he wanted higher interest rates and, by inference, a recession to contain inflation.

Dr Brash commented, As I have often said in public, I regard the present mix of monetary conditions as less than optimal, with the exchange rate too high, so that too much pressure is being exerted on export industries.

I have also said that conversely not enough disinflationary pressure is being exerted on the domestic economy. As a result I would prefer a different mix, with a lower exchange rate and higher domestic interest rates, and I told the Alliance caucus that.

However, it is totally misleading to suggest that I told the Alliance that the only way of easing upward pressure on the exchange rate was through a recession. This I reject. The inflation target set for the Reserve Bank is 0 to 3 percent annual underlying inflation.
A breach below 0 percent would be just as serious as a breach above 3 percent. The aim of monetary policy is to avoid boom-bust cycles.
In fact, the rising pressure on the exchange rate will abate over time. This will happen because:
* either, inflationary pressures within New Zealand will fall back, which will enable domestic monetary policy to be eased;
* or, inflationary pressures abroad will rise, which will prompt other countries to tighten their monetary policies, thus reducing the gap between interest rates in New Zealand and those abroad;
* or, increasing concerns about the balance of payments deficit will see capital inflows into New Zealand diminish. None of these necessarily imply a recession.

Note also that since New Zealand first achieved sub-2 percent inflation in 1991, we have enjoyed our longest period of unbroken economic growth for many years, with the greatest fall in unemployment of any developed country over that period, Dr Brash concluded.
